name: Venus
description: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and the hottest planet in the Solar System due to its extreme greenhouse effect. It is often called Earth's twin due to similar size and mass, but its surface is a hellish 464°C with crushing atmospheric pressure.
atmosphere: 96.5% CO₂, 3.5% Nitrogen, trace sulfuric acid clouds
surface: Volcanic plains, mountain ranges, thousands of volcanoes
summary: Venus is Earth's closest planetary neighbor in size but utterly hostile. Its runaway greenhouse effect has created surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead, constant cloud cover of sulfuric acid, and crushing atmospheric pressure. Yet Venus may once have had liquid water oceans billions of years ago.
interesting_facts: Venus rotates backwards (east to west) compared to most planets
A day on Venus is longer than its year — 243 Earth days to rotate, 225 days to orbit the Sun
Venus is the hottest planet at 464°C, despite not being closest to the Sun
Venus has the densest atmosphere of any rocky planet — 92 times Earth's pressure
Venus may have had liquid water oceans 2–3 billion years ago
Venus has over 1,600 major volcanoes — more than any other planet
The Soviet Venera missions landed on Venus in the 1970s–80s (the landers survived only minutes to hours)
Venus is the brightest natural object in the night sky after the Moon
The ESA EnVision mission and NASA DAVINCI will return to Venus in the 2030s

faq.q: Why is Venus the hottest planet?
faq.a: Venus has a thick atmosphere of 96.5% CO₂ that traps heat through the greenhouse effect, raising surface temperatures to 464°C — hotter than Mercury, despite being farther from the Sun.
Yes! Venus rotates in the opposite direction to most planets (retrograde rotation). This means the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east on Venus.

No. Venus's surface has crushing atmospheric pressure (92× Earth), temperatures of 464°C, and clouds of sulfuric acid. Future missions may explore Venus's upper atmosphere where conditions are more Earth-like.
Venus has no liquid water today. However, models suggest Venus may have had shallow oceans billions of years ago before a runaway greenhouse effect evaporated them all.

faq.q: Why is Venus called Earth's twin?
faq.a: Venus and Earth are similar in size (Venus is 95% of Earth's diameter), mass (82% of Earth's), density, and bulk composition. They likely formed from similar materials in the early solar system.

faq.q: Has any spacecraft landed on Venus?
faq.a: Yes! The Soviet Venera program (1961–1985) successfully landed 10 probes on Venus. Venera 7 was the first successful Venus lander in 1970. The landers survived only minutes to hours due to extreme conditions.

faq.q: How long is a day on Venus?
faq.a: Venus rotates so slowly that a solar day (sunrise to sunrise) is 116.75 Earth days. Its rotation period is 243 Earth days — longer than its year of 225 days.
Venus has a silicate rocky mantle, possibly a partially liquid iron core, and a heavily cratered surface covered in volcanic plains and highland regions.
Yes! Venus is the brightest natural object in the night sky after the Moon, often visible as the 'Morning Star' or 'Evening Star' near dawn or dusk.

faq.q: What missions are planned for Venus?
faq.a: NASA's DAVINCI (2031) will send an atmospheric probe, and ESA's EnVision (2030s) will orbit Venus with radar mapping. Both aim to understand Venus's past and why it differs so dramatically from Earth.
